analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment fund managers' performance profits as ordinary income instead of at lower capital-gains rates.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 13 senators, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2015 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships are paid largely in 'carried interest' — a share of the fund's profits. Under current law that income is taxed at the long-term capital gains rate, about 20%, instead of the top ordinary income rate of about 39.6%. This bill would reclassify that income as ordinary income, subject it to self-employment tax, and raise the penalty for underreporting it, while carving out genuine invested capital and certain family partnerships.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers generally, who would see more revenue and a fairer tax code, and ordinary wage earners whose salaries are already taxed as ordinary income at higher rates than this fund-manager income.

how_it_helps.text: Treats the net capital gain on an 'investment services partnership interest' — a fund manager's carried interest — as ordinary income rather than capital gain, raising the tax rate on that compensation to ordinary rates [S2].

Subjects income from these partnership interests to self-employment taxes, which currently do not apply to carried-interest profits, so fund managers would contribute to Social Security and Medicare on that income like other workers [S2].
Increases the underpayment penalty to 40% for tax avoidance involving these interests, strengthening enforcement [S2].

Preserves the capital-gains treatment for a manager's genuine invested capital ('qualified capital interests') and exempts certain family partnerships, targeting only compensation earned for investment services [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, real estate, and venture capital fund managers, who would pay ordinary income rates and self-employment tax on performance-based compensation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: Fund managers and many economists argue carried interest is a genuine return on risk taken with capital committed to long-term illiquid investments, and that raising its rate would discourage the investment that funds provide to businesses, real estate, and infrastructure.

The bill reaches beyond Wall Street funds: real estate held for rental or investment and commodities are 'specified assets' under the bill, so real estate and energy partnerships that use carried interest would also face higher taxes, and critics argue costs would partly pass through to rents and development [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill closes a tax preference that overwhelmingly benefits some of the highest-earning people in the country, whose compensation is taxed more lightly than a nurse's salary. The main honest objection is economic: fund managers play an active role in businesses and real estate, and some argue higher taxes would reduce that investment. The bill tries to limit collateral damage by exempting genuine invested capital and family partnerships, but it would still hit real estate and energy deals beyond the hedge funds usually discussed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act on June 25, 2015, joined by eight original cosponsors including Sens. Whitehouse, Warren, Franken, Sanders, Reed, Hirono, Manchin, and Blumenthal [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the only action ever taken [S5].
The bill accumulated 12 cosponsors (11 Democrats and 1 independent) but the Finance Committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, real estate, and venture capital managers are better off: because the bill never moved, they kept paying the roughly 20% capital gains rate on carried interest instead of ordinary income rates, and the Treasury forgoes the revenue it would have collected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers who kept the tax break

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 25, 2015 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate industries
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed carried-interest tax increases in this era and defended the capital-gains treatment, which fund managers' trade groups lobbied to preserve.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors were Democrats or independents, and the Republican-controlled Senate took no action on the bill during the entire 114th Congress.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: The bill taxes their carried-interest compensation as ordinary income and applies self-employment tax, directly reducing their after-tax pay. Their interest in keeping the lower rate runs against ordinary wage earners, who pay higher rates on salary.

Real estate held for rental or investment is a 'specified asset' under the bill, so carried interests in real estate and energy deals would also be taxed as ordinary income. Developers argue this raises the cost of building and renovating property.

Venture capitalists' profit shares from investing in startups would be taxed at ordinary rates. Industry groups argue this would reduce funding for new companies, while supporters argue their compensation is still work income.
